intro.body: Repeat prescription support helps you stay on regular medicines without gaps — with pharmacist advice on reorder timing and EPS nomination.
Managing ongoing medicines is easier when repeat ordering is coordinated with your GP surgery and pharmacy team.
Community pharmacy repeat services cover EPS setup, reorder reminders and supply planning — so treatment continues safely between GP reviews.
A structured repeat process reduces missed doses from running out — with pharmacist checks when medicines change.
From electronic prescription nomination to collection or delivery, repeat services keep long-term treatment on track with clear next steps.

problem.heading: Why Repeat Ordering Matters
problem.body: Running out of regular medicines can cause avoidable harm — especially for conditions such as asthma, diabetes, heart disease and mental health. Repeat processes need GP authorisation and timely reordering.

problem.heading: Medicines Continuity Risks
problem.body: Gaps in supply affect adherence and symptom control. Delays often happen when reordering is left too late or nomination is not updated after switching pharmacy.

problem.heading: Understanding Repeat Prescriptions
problem.body: Repeat items are authorised by your GP for a set period — not indefinitely. Pharmacy teams advise on timing but cannot authorise new repeats without surgery approval.

problem.heading: Common Repeat Challenges
problem.body: Patients often struggle with EPS nomination, holiday supply, or medicines started by a hospital. Pharmacists signpost to GP when authorisation or clinical review is needed.

problem.heading: Staying On Treatment Safely
problem.body: Consistent supply supports long-term health outcomes. Pharmacy repeat support complements GP care — it does not replace medical review when symptoms or treatment change.

benefits.heading: Benefits Of Repeat Support
benefits.body: Pharmacy-led repeat coordination offers convenient reorder advice, EPS nomination help and supply planning without always needing a GP appointment for routine items.

benefits.heading: What The Service Delivers
benefits.body: You receive practical help with repeat ordering, clarity on authorisation status, and pharmacist advice when medicines are new or changed.

benefits.heading: Practical Advantages
benefits.body: Repeat services fit around everyday routines. Pharmacists explain when to reorder, how EPS works, and what to do if an item is not yet authorised.

benefits.heading: Patient-Focused Continuity
benefits.body: The service focuses on keeping treatment on track — with professional oversight when prescriptions are clinically screened before supply.

benefits.heading: Accessible Medicines Management
benefits.body: Community pharmacy access lowers barriers for people who find GP phone lines busy or who need local support coordinating repeats.

eligibility.heading: Who Can Use Repeat Services
eligibility.body: Patients with GP-authorised repeat prescriptions may use pharmacy repeat support. New medicines, dose changes and acute symptoms need GP review — not repeat reordering alone.
bullets: Not for emergency supply without assessment

eligibility.heading: Repeat Suitability
eligibility.body: Suitability depends on your prescription status. Pharmacists confirm whether items are authorised, on hold, or need surgery contact before supply.

eligibility.heading: Before You Start
eligibility.body: Ensure your GP surgery has authorised repeats and your nomination is current if using EPS. Share medicine changes promptly so records stay accurate.

eligibility.heading: Eligibility Overview
eligibility.body: Repeat support suits patients on stable long-term medicines. Unstable conditions, new symptoms or hospital-only medicines may need GP clarification first.

eligibility.heading: Is This Right For Me
eligibility.body: If you are unsure whether an item is on repeat or authorised, contact the pharmacy team. They advise on next steps and surgery liaison when needed.

howItWorks.heading: How Repeat Ordering Works
howItWorks.body: The process covers checking authorisation, submitting or receiving the prescription, clinical screening and supply — with advice on when to reorder next.

howItWorks.heading: Your Reorder Steps
howItWorks.body: Request repeats before you run low — typically seven to ten days ahead for items needing ordering. Pharmacists track supply and advise if GP authorisation is pending.

howItWorks.heading: The Repeat Pathway
howItWorks.body: Repeats follow a structured pathway: authorisation check, prescription receipt, dispensing and handover. Diagnosis and new prescriptions remain with your GP.

howItWorks.heading: What Happens When You Reorder
howItWorks.body: The pharmacy team checks whether your surgery has released the prescription. Delays may need surgery liaison — you are kept informed on timing.

howItWorks.heading: From Request To Collection
howItWorks.body: Allow time for GP authorisation on each reorder cycle. Once received, clinical checks and preparation follow before handover or delivery.

preparationGuide.heading: Preparing To Reorder
preparationGuide.body: Reorder before your medicines run out. Note any dose changes, new OTC products, or upcoming travel that may affect supply needs.
bullets: Reorder seven to ten days early

preparationGuide.heading: Before Your First Repeat Setup
preparationGuide.body: Nominate your pharmacy for EPS with your GP surgery. Bring your repeat slip, medicines list and allergy information for accurate records.

preparationGuide.heading: What To Bring Or Share
preparationGuide.body: Share hospital discharge letters if medicines changed recently. Carers should confirm proxy collection rules — especially for controlled drugs.

preparationGuide.heading: Holiday And Travel Supply
preparationGuide.body: Plan holiday supply early — GP authorisation may be needed for extra quantity. Pharmacists advise on timing and documentation.

preparationGuide.heading: Staying Organised
preparationGuide.body: Use a medicines diary or dosette tray if helpful. Set reminders to reorder and keep one week's buffer where possible.

trustSafety.heading: Safety And Professional Standards
trustSafety.body: Pharmacy teams cannot supply repeats without valid GP authorisation. Clinical checks apply before every supply — repeats are not automatic without prescriber approval.

trustSafety.heading: When To Contact Your GP
trustSafety.body: New symptoms, dose changes, treatment not working, or medicines started in hospital need GP review — not repeat reordering alone.

trustSafety.heading: Professional Insight
trustSafety.body: Reliable repeat management works best when patients reorder early, keep nomination updated, and tell the pharmacy about all medicines including OTC products.

trustSafety.heading: Trust And Clinical Governance
trustSafety.body: Regulated pharmacy teams follow dispensing governance on every repeat supply, with documented advice and surgery liaison when authorisation is delayed.

patientEducation.heading: Understanding EPS
patientEducation.body: Electronic Prescription Service sends prescriptions from your GP to a nominated pharmacy digitally — reducing paper delays when nomination is set up correctly.

patientEducation.heading: Patient Education
patientEducation.body: Educational guidance covers reorder timing, authorisation cycles, and when GP involvement is needed instead of routine repeat supply.

patientEducation.heading: Medicines Continuity Basics
patientEducation.body: Understanding why gaps matter helps you reorder on time and report changes promptly — supporting safer long-term treatment.

patientEducation.heading: Your Role In Safe Repeats
patientEducation.body: Keep an updated medicines list, reorder before running out, and ask the pharmacy if authorisation seems delayed.

mythVsFact.heading: Myths Vs Facts
mythVsFact.body: Evidence-based repeat advice separates common misconceptions from accurate information:
bullets: Myth: Repeats renew automatically forever. Fact: GP authorisation expires and must be renewed.
Myth: Pharmacy can authorise new repeats. Fact: Only your GP surgery authorises repeat prescriptions.
Myth: EPS means instant supply. Fact: Clinical checks and GP release still take time.

mythVsFact.heading: Repeat Misconceptions
mythVsFact.body: Clear facts help you manage medicines safely:
bullets: Myth: Running out is fine for a few days. Fact: Gaps can harm control of chronic conditions.
Myth: Switching pharmacy needs no GP update. Fact: Update EPS nomination with your surgery.
Myth: Pharmacists change repeat doses. Fact: Dose changes need GP prescription.

mythVsFact.heading: Medicines Supply Facts
mythVsFact.body: Separating myths from facts supports safer repeat use:
bullets: Myth: All repeats are NHS-funded. Fact: Some items may incur charges or be private.
Myth: Carers need no ID for controlled drugs. Fact: ID and authorisation rules often apply.
Myth: Holiday extras need no GP notice. Fact: Extra quantity usually needs authorisation.

mythVsFact.heading: Common Repeat Myths
bullets: Myth: Hospital medicines auto-join repeats. Fact: GP must add them to your repeat list.
Myth: OTC products do not affect repeats. Fact: Interactions must be declared.
Myth: Delivery replaces clinical checks. Fact: Same governance applies before supply.

faqs.question: How do I set up repeat prescriptions?
faqs.answer: Ask your GP surgery to authorise repeats and nominate a pharmacy for EPS. The pharmacy team can guide you through nomination and first supply.

faqs.question: What is EPS nomination?
faqs.answer: Electronic Prescription Service sends prescriptions digitally from your GP to your nominated pharmacy, reducing paper handling delays.

faqs.question: How early should I reorder repeats?
faqs.answer: Reorder seven to ten days before you run out — sooner for items that need ordering in. This allows GP authorisation and dispensing time.

faqs.question: Can the pharmacy authorise my repeats?
faqs.answer: No — only your GP surgery authorises repeat prescriptions. The pharmacy supplies once authorisation is received.

faqs.question: What if my repeat is not ready?
faqs.answer: Delays may mean GP authorisation is pending. The pharmacy team can liaise with your surgery and advise on timing.

faqs.question: Can someone collect repeats for me?
faqs.answer: Yes in most cases — controlled drugs may need ID and written authorisation. Confirm requirements with the pharmacy.

faqs.question: How do I switch pharmacy for repeats?
faqs.answer: Update EPS nomination with your GP surgery and inform both pharmacies to avoid duplicate or missed supply.

faqs.question: What if my medicines changed in hospital?
faqs.answer: Contact your GP so repeats are updated. Do not assume hospital medicines are automatically on your repeat list.

faqs.question: Can I get extra supply for holiday?
faqs.answer: Often yes with GP authorisation for additional quantity. Request early to allow surgery approval and dispensing.

faqs.question: Do repeats expire?
faqs.answer: Yes — GP repeat authorisation runs for a set period. Your surgery reviews and renews when appropriate.

faqs.question: Is repeat ordering free?
faqs.answer: NHS prescription charges apply unless you are exempt. Some items may be private — the pharmacy confirms at supply.

faqs.question: What if I run out completely?
faqs.answer: Contact the pharmacy urgently. Emergency supply may be possible in limited circumstances — not a substitute for timely reordering.

faqs.question: Can I use delivery for repeats?
faqs.answer: Many pharmacies offer delivery for repeats where available. Ask about eligibility, timing and any charges.

faqs.question: Should I tell the pharmacy about OTC medicines?
faqs.answer: Yes — OTC and herbal products can interact with prescribed medicines. Share your full list for safe clinical checks.

faqs.question: When should I see my GP instead of reordering?
faqs.answer: New symptoms, side effects, dose changes, or treatment not working need GP review — not routine repeat supply alone.
